did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title attributes it to David and describes his escape after he changed his behavior before Abimelech, who drove him away, and he left.

Did you know? David emphasizes that praising the Lord is not merely a response to a moment of success: he says that he will bless the Lord “at all times” and that His praise will “always” be in his mouth.
Did you know? David does not keep his praise to himself, but calls others to join him: “Magnify the Lord with me” and “let us exalt His name together.”
Did you know? In this verse, the Lord is portrayed as a protector surrounding those who fear Him, using the image of an angel encamped around them and delivering them.
Did you know? The expression “Taste and see” presents the goodness of the Lord as something people are invited to experience and know personally, not merely hear about.
Did you know? The psalm contrasts lions, which may go hungry, with those who seek the Lord, who are said to lack no good thing.
Did you know? This is where a direct teaching section begins: David addresses the “children” and teaches them what it means to fear the Lord.
Did you know? According to the psalm, a good life begins with control of one’s speech: a person is called to keep his tongue from evil and to turn away from deceitful speech.
Did you know? Peace is presented here not merely as a condition to wait for, but as a goal to seek and pursue actively.

Did you know? The psalm does not promise the righteous a life without trouble; on the contrary, it says that “many are the afflictions of the righteous,” but adds that the Lord delivers him from them all.
